newsitem.title: USA: Iraq's Aziz to meet UN sanctions panel head Monday.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's Aziz to meet UN sanctions panel head Monday.

text.p: Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz will meet with the head of the U.N. sanctions committee Monday afternoon to discuss implementation of the second round of the "oil-for-food" accord, Iraqi officials and Western diplomats said.
Aziz was scheduled to meet the sanctions chairman, Portugal's Ambassador Antonio Monteiro at 4:45 p.m. (2045 GMT) at the official Iraqi residence in New York.

Aziz is to leave town Tuesday after spending more than a week in New York, obstensibly to attend the U.N. Earth Summit and secondly to rally support for lifting six-year-old sanctions slapped on Baghdad after the 1990 Kuwait invasion.
Western diplomats on the sanctions committee said the meeting was planned during last Friday's panel meeting.
"They will generally talk about Resolution 986 (the terms of the oil accord), and when we should expect to see the distribution plan," said the diplomat.

Even though Iraq had the oil deal renewed for a second 180-day tranche from June 8, the U.N. has yet to receive the necessary aid distribution plan, which would trigger the process for restarting stalled oil contract signings and liftings.
Iraq must also submit a pricing formula before oil sales recommence.

Best estimates from U.N. officials and recent Iraqi statements point to Iraq submitting a finalized distribution plan within 10 days. Working out the bureacratic kinks could extend the actual start of new liftings into August.
On Monday, Iraqi diplomat and lead negotiator for the oil accord, Abdul Amir al-Anbari, reiterated his belief that oil would flow again in early August.
The Western diplomat on the sanction panel said he did not expect to see the Iraqi distribution plan before July 7 at the earliest.
Aziz told Reuters on Sunday that Baghdad had completed a distribution plan, but was waiting for a U.N. team to come to Iraq and work out details.
"As far as I know they (the U.N. and Iraq) are meeting now and talking over the plan," said the Western diplomat.
Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude for a 180-day period, mainly to buy food and medicine for civilians suffering under trade sanctions.
